Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative primarily unfolds as a vivid, real-time scene, grounding the reader in the present moment through sensory details (the cold hallway, the smell of old cleaning supplies and quince, the sandy texture of the dried fruit) and physical actions (opening the stuck door with her hip, walking into the kitchen). 

At the same time, the writer seamlessly weaves in brief moments of summary and exposition to provide crucial context without slowing down the pace. For example, the opening lines quickly summarize the interaction with the neighbor, and the detail about her body remembering how to open the door after twenty years effortlessly delivers character history. The state of the emptied fridge and the shriveled fruit also serve as subtle environmental exposition, hinting at a recent loss or departure without needing a dry info-dump. This careful balance keeps the story engaging, atmospheric, and emotionally resonant.
